Reference: Arkolakis, Eckert and Shi (2023)

Model Setting

A combinatorial discrete choice problem (CDCP) is the problem of choosing the combination of items that maximizes an objective function when the value of each item depends on which other items are also chosen. A multinational firm selecting production locations is the leading example: plants in Germany and the United States may create scale economies that raise the value of both, while plants in Germany and France may cannibalize each other in the European market. Without structure on the objective function the problem is NP-hard and the decision maker must evaluate all 2∣L∣2^{|L|}2∣L∣ combinations, which is more than one million with only twenty items. The paper develops an exact solution method that applies whenever the objective satisfies a single crossing differences condition, a condition weaker than requiring items to be complements (supermodularity) or substitutes (submodularity). The method discards suboptimal combinations without computing their payoffs, always recovers the global optimum, and extends to heterogeneous agents, for whom it delivers the exact policy function mapping each type to its optimal combination. It builds on Jia (2008), whose method covers only the complements case and falls back on brute force over whatever part of the domain is left; the paper extends the elimination logic to substitutes, replaces the brute-force step with a branching procedure, and avoids discretizing agent heterogeneity.

The application is a general equilibrium model of multinational production (MP) in which heterogeneous firms choose sets of production locations subject to fixed costs. An additional plant raises firm-level scale economies but cannibalizes the firm's other plants, and a single ratio of two elasticities determines which force wins. The model is calibrated to trade, affiliate sales and affiliate counts for 32 OECD and European countries, for 37 different degrees of complementarity or substitutability. The method is up to four to five orders of magnitude faster than brute force and one to two orders of magnitude faster than the Jia (2008) approach on a productivity grid, and it removes a discretization error in aggregate flows that exceeds 20 percent even on a grid of 16,384 points. Quantitatively, the stronger the complementarity among locations, the more the welfare gains from MP concentrate in the headquarter countries of the most productive firms, and some countries that mainly host foreign affiliates lose; with substitutability, gains are positive and more even.

Defining the Problem

Let LLL be a finite set of items (locations) indexed by ℓ\ellℓ, let P(L)\mathcal{P}(L)P(L) be the set of all subsets of LLL, and let f:P(L)→Rf:\mathcal{P}(L)\to\mathbb{R}f:P(L)→R be the objective function. A decision set is some L∈P(L)\mathcal{L}\in\mathcal{P}(L)L∈P(L). The marginal value operator measures the contribution of item ℓ\ellℓ given a decision set:

Dℓf(L)≡f(L∪{ℓ})−f(L∖{ℓ})(6.3.4.1)D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\equiv f\left(\mathcal{L}\cup\{\ell\}\right)-f\left(\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}\right) \tag{6.3.4.1}Dℓ​f(L)≡f(L∪{ℓ})−f(L∖{ℓ})(6.3.4.1)

A CDCP is the maximization problem:

L⋆≡arg⁡max⁡L∈P(L)f(L)(6.3.4.2)\mathcal{L}^\star\equiv\arg\max_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathcal{P}(L)}f(\mathcal{L}) \tag{6.3.4.2}L⋆≡argL∈P(L)max​f(L)(6.3.4.2)

in which choices are interdependent, that is, there exist ℓ∈L\ell\in Lℓ∈L and L,L′∈P(L)\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}'\in\mathcal{P}(L)L,L′∈P(L) with Dℓf(L)≠Dℓf(L′)D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\neq D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')Dℓ​f(L)=Dℓ​f(L′). If marginal values did not depend on the decision set, the problem would reduce to ∣L∣|L|∣L∣ independent binary decisions.

Single Crossing Differences in Choices

The method applies when fff satisfies single crossing differences in choices (SCD-C). For every ℓ∈L\ell\in Lℓ∈L and all decision sets with L⊂L′\mathcal{L}\subset\mathcal{L}'L⊂L′, the two versions of the condition are:

SCD-C from above:Dℓf(L′)≥0  ⇒  Dℓf(L)≥0SCD-C from below:Dℓf(L)≥0  ⇒  Dℓf(L′)≥0(6.3.4.3)\begin{aligned} \text{SCD-C from above:}\qquad&D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')\geq 0\;\Rightarrow\;D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\geq 0\\ \text{SCD-C from below:}\qquad&D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\geq 0\;\Rightarrow\;D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')\geq 0 \end{aligned} \tag{6.3.4.3}SCD-C from above:SCD-C from below:​Dℓ​f(L′)≥0⇒Dℓ​f(L)≥0Dℓ​f(L)≥0⇒Dℓ​f(L′)≥0​(6.3.4.3)

Along any sequence of expanding decision sets, the marginal value of an item therefore crosses zero at most once. Under SCD-C from below, an item with non-negative marginal value keeps a non-negative marginal value when other items are added (a generalization of complements). Under SCD-C from above, it keeps a non-negative marginal value when other items are removed (a generalization of substitutes). Supermodularity, which requires Dℓf(L)≤Dℓf(L′)D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\leq D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')Dℓ​f(L)≤Dℓ​f(L′) for all L⊆L′\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{L}'L⊆L′ and all ℓ\ellℓ, is sufficient for SCD-C from below, and submodularity, which reverses the inequality, is sufficient for SCD-C from above. Neither is necessary, because SCD-C restricts only the sign of the marginal value and lets its size rise or fall arbitrarily. For example, a Canadian plant may lower the marginal value of a firm's US plant by cannibalizing its Canadian sales while raising the marginal value of its German plant through scale. This violates supermodularity but is consistent with SCD-C from below as long as the US plant's marginal value stays weakly positive.

The Squeezing Procedure

A pair of bounding sets [L‾,L‾][\underline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{L}}][L​,L] consists of a lower and an upper bounding set with L‾⊆L⋆⊆L‾\underline{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}L​⊆L⋆⊆L. The pair defines a subdomain of the problem: every item in L‾\underline{\mathcal{L}}L​ is known to be chosen, and every item outside L‾\overline{\mathcal{L}}L is known not to be chosen. The original domain corresponds to the domain bounding sets [∅,L][\emptyset,L][∅,L]. The central object is the mapping that returns the items with non-negative marginal value given a decision set:

Φ(L)≡{ℓ∈L∣Dℓf(L)≥0}(6.3.4.4)\Phi(\mathcal{L})\equiv\left\{\ell\in L\mid D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\geq 0\right\} \tag{6.3.4.4}Φ(L)≡{ℓ∈L∣Dℓ​f(L)≥0}(6.3.4.4)

It is the discrete analogue of a first-order condition, and Φ(L⋆)=L⋆\Phi(\mathcal{L}^\star)=\mathcal{L}^\starΦ(L⋆)=L⋆ by construction, where L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ is taken to include the items over which the agent is indifferent. The squeezing step is the mapping:

S([L,L′])≡[inf⁡{Φ(L),Φ(L′)},  sup⁡{Φ(L),Φ(L′)}](6.3.4.5)S\left(\left[\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}'\right]\right)\equiv\left[\inf\left\{\Phi(\mathcal{L}),\Phi(\mathcal{L}')\right\},\;\sup\left\{\Phi(\mathcal{L}),\Phi(\mathcal{L}')\right\}\right] \tag{6.3.4.5}S([L,L′])≡[inf{Φ(L),Φ(L′)},sup{Φ(L),Φ(L′)}](6.3.4.5)

The mapping Φ\PhiΦ is monotone if and only if fff satisfies SCD-C. Under SCD-C from below, L⊂L′\mathcal{L}\subset\mathcal{L}'L⊂L′ implies Φ(L)⊆Φ(L′)\Phi(\mathcal{L})\subseteq\Phi(\mathcal{L}')Φ(L)⊆Φ(L′), so Φ\PhiΦ is order-preserving. Under SCD-C from above, L⊂L′\mathcal{L}\subset\mathcal{L}'L⊂L′ implies Φ(L′)⊆Φ(L)\Phi(\mathcal{L}')\subseteq\Phi(\mathcal{L})Φ(L′)⊆Φ(L), so Φ\PhiΦ is order-reversing. When the type of SCD-C is known, the squeezing step therefore simplifies to:

from above:S([L‾,L‾])=[Φ(L‾),Φ(L‾)]from below:S([L‾,L‾])=[Φ(L‾),Φ(L‾)](6.3.4.6)\begin{aligned} \text{from above:}\qquad&S\left(\left[\underline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{L}}\right]\right)=\left[\Phi\left(\overline{\mathcal{L}}\right),\Phi\left(\underline{\mathcal{L}}\right)\right]\\ \text{from below:}\qquad&S\left(\left[\underline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{L}}\right]\right)=\left[\Phi\left(\underline{\mathcal{L}}\right),\Phi\left(\overline{\mathcal{L}}\right)\right] \end{aligned} \tag{6.3.4.6}from above:from below:​S([L​,L])=[Φ(L),Φ(L​)]S([L​,L])=[Φ(L​),Φ(L)]​(6.3.4.6)

Theorem 1. If fff exhibits SCD-C from above or from below, iteratively applying the squeezing step to the domain bounding sets [∅,L][\emptyset,L][∅,L] yields a sequence of bounding sets:

∅=L‾(0)⊆⋯⊆L‾(k)⊆L‾(k+1)⊆L⋆⊆L‾(k+1)⊆L‾(k)⊆⋯⊆L‾(0)=L(6.3.4.7)\emptyset=\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(0)}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}\subseteq\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k+1)}\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k+1)}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(0)}=L \tag{6.3.4.7}∅=L​(0)⊆⋯⊆L​(k)⊆L​(k+1)⊆L⋆⊆L(k+1)⊆L(k)⊆⋯⊆L(0)=L(6.3.4.7)

where kkk is the iteration count, and the iteration converges in K≤∣L∣K\leq|L|K≤∣L∣ applications.

The intuition is that under SCD-C the marginal value of an item only needs to be evaluated at the two extreme decision sets that are still admissible. Take SCD-C from above. The upper bounding set is the least favorable environment for item ℓ\ellℓ, because all potential substitutes are present. If Dℓf(L‾)≥0D_\ell f(\overline{\mathcal{L}})\geq 0Dℓ​f(L)≥0, then single crossing gives Dℓf(L⋆)≥0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}^\star)\geq 0Dℓ​f(L⋆)≥0 since L⋆⊆L‾\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}L⋆⊆L, so ℓ\ellℓ belongs to the optimum and every combination that excludes ℓ\ellℓ is discarded without being evaluated. The lower bounding set is the most favorable environment. If Dℓf(L‾)<0D_\ell f(\underline{\mathcal{L}})<0Dℓ​f(L​)<0, then Dℓf(L⋆)<0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}^\star)<0Dℓ​f(L⋆)<0, so ℓ\ellℓ is not in the optimum and every combination that includes it is discarded. Under SCD-C from below the roles are reversed: an item that is valuable even at the lower bounding set is always included, and one that is not valuable even at the upper bounding set is always excluded. Formally, applying an order-reversing Φ\PhiΦ to L‾⊆L⋆⊆L‾\underline{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}L​⊆L⋆⊆L and using Φ(L⋆)=L⋆\Phi(\mathcal{L}^\star)=\mathcal{L}^\starΦ(L⋆)=L⋆ gives Φ(L‾)⊆L⋆⊆Φ(L‾)\Phi(\overline{\mathcal{L}})\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\Phi(\underline{\mathcal{L}})Φ(L)⊆L⋆⊆Φ(L​), so the output of a squeezing step is again a valid pair of bounding sets. Starting from [∅,L][\emptyset,L][∅,L], two applications give:

∅⊆Φ(L)⊆Φ(Φ(∅))⊆L⋆⊆Φ(Φ(L))⊆Φ(∅)⊆L(6.3.4.8)\emptyset\subseteq\Phi(L)\subseteq\Phi\left(\Phi(\emptyset)\right)\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\Phi\left(\Phi(L)\right)\subseteq\Phi(\emptyset)\subseteq L \tag{6.3.4.8}∅⊆Φ(L)⊆Φ(Φ(∅))⊆L⋆⊆Φ(Φ(L))⊆Φ(∅)⊆L(6.3.4.8)

because ∅⊆Φ(L)\emptyset\subseteq\Phi(L)∅⊆Φ(L) implies Φ(Φ(L))⊆Φ(∅)\Phi(\Phi(L))\subseteq\Phi(\emptyset)Φ(Φ(L))⊆Φ(∅), and symmetrically for the lower bound. By induction the bounds tighten weakly at every step. Each non-terminal iteration adds at least one item to the lower bounding set or removes at least one from the upper bounding set, so there are at most ∣L∣|L|∣L∣ steps. The iteration to convergence is the squeezing procedure, written SKS^KSK, and its output SK([∅,L])S^K([\emptyset,L])SK([∅,L]) is the pair of reduced bounding sets. If the two sets coincide, the optimum is found.

The link to fixed-point theory explains why the substitutes case is harder. With an order-preserving Φ\PhiΦ, the theorem of Tarski (1955) guarantees a smallest and a largest fixed point, Linf⁡\mathcal{L}^{\inf}Linf and Lsup⁡\mathcal{L}^{\sup}Lsup, and iterating Φ\PhiΦ from ∅\emptyset∅ and from LLL converges to them (Kleene's fixed point theorem). This is the method of Jia (2008), and the squeezing procedure coincides with it, so that SK([∅,L])=[Linf⁡,Lsup⁡]S^K([\emptyset,L])=[\mathcal{L}^{\inf},\mathcal{L}^{\sup}]SK([∅,L])=[Linf,Lsup]; the paper adds that SCD-C from below, not supermodularity, is the necessary and sufficient condition for it to work. With an order-reversing Φ\PhiΦ, iterating from either extreme may oscillate. With two perfectly substitutable locations, each profitable alone and neither profitable alongside the other, Φ(∅)={USA,CAN}\Phi(\emptyset)=\{\text{USA},\text{CAN}\}Φ(∅)={USA,CAN} and Φ({USA,CAN})=∅\Phi(\{\text{USA},\text{CAN}\})=\emptysetΦ({USA,CAN})=∅. The iteration converges instead to a fixed edge, a pair [L,L′][\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}'][L,L′] with L⊆L′\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{L}'L⊆L′, L=Φ(L′)\mathcal{L}=\Phi(\mathcal{L}')L=Φ(L′) and L′=Φ(L)\mathcal{L}'=\Phi(\mathcal{L})L′=Φ(L). Klimes (1981) shows that an order-reversing map always has an extreme fixed edge that nests all others (because Φ∘Φ\Phi\circ\PhiΦ∘Φ is order-preserving), and under SCD-C from above the squeezing procedure converges to it. In both cases SSS itself is an order-preserving mapping on pairs of sets. The procedure converges to [L⋆,L⋆][\mathcal{L}^\star,\mathcal{L}^\star][L⋆,L⋆] if and only if L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ is the unique fixed point (from below) or the unique fixed edge (from above) of Φ\PhiΦ.

The Branching Procedure

When the reduced bounding sets satisfy L‾⊂L‾\underline{\mathcal{L}}\subset\overline{\mathcal{L}}L​⊂L, the branching step picks an undetermined item ℓ∈L‾∖L‾\ell\in\overline{\mathcal{L}}\setminus\underline{\mathcal{L}}ℓ∈L∖L​ and creates two branches, one that imposes that ℓ\ellℓ is included and one that imposes that it is excluded. Each branch is a restricted CDCP of choosing L⊆(L‾∖L‾)∖{ℓ}\mathcal{L}\subseteq(\overline{\mathcal{L}}\setminus\underline{\mathcal{L}})\setminus\{\ell\}L⊆(L∖L​)∖{ℓ} to maximize the modified objective:

f~(L)≡f(L∪L‾∪{ℓ})on the branch that includes ℓf~(L)≡f(L∪L‾)on the branch that excludes ℓ(6.3.4.9)\begin{aligned} \tilde{f}(\mathcal{L})&\equiv f\left(\mathcal{L}\cup\underline{\mathcal{L}}\cup\{\ell\}\right)\qquad\text{on the branch that includes }\ell\\ \tilde{f}(\mathcal{L})&\equiv f\left(\mathcal{L}\cup\underline{\mathcal{L}}\right)\qquad\text{on the branch that excludes }\ell \end{aligned} \tag{6.3.4.9}f~​(L)f~​(L)​≡f(L∪L​∪{ℓ})on the branch that includes ℓ≡f(L∪L​)on the branch that excludes ℓ​(6.3.4.9)

The squeezing procedure is applied to each restricted problem, and the resulting bounding sets are translated back to the original problem by adding L‾\underline{\mathcal{L}}L​ (and ℓ\ellℓ on the including branch). A branch whose bounding sets coincide has found a conditionally optimal decision set; otherwise the branching step is applied again on that branch. The recursion builds a tree, and with Λ([L‾,L‾])\Lambda([\underline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{L}}])Λ([L​,L]) denoting the collection of conditionally optimal sets at its terminal nodes, the solution is:

L⋆=arg⁡max⁡L∈Λ([L‾,L‾])f(L)(6.3.4.10)\mathcal{L}^\star=\arg\max_{\mathcal{L}\in\Lambda\left(\left[\underline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{L}}\right]\right)}f(\mathcal{L}) \tag{6.3.4.10}L⋆=argL∈Λ([L​,L])max​f(L)(6.3.4.10)

The collection may depend on the order in which items are selected, but it always contains the global maximum, and every fixed point of Φ\PhiΦ is a terminal node. Branching thus applies the brute-force logic one item at a time and squeezes after each split, so the objective is evaluated only at a handful of candidates. In the worst case, when squeezing eliminates nothing on any branch, it evaluates the same sets as brute force.

Heterogeneous Agents and the Policy Function

Now let f:P(L)×R→Rf:\mathcal{P}(L)\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}f:P(L)×R→R depend on a scalar agent type zzz and be continuous in zzz. The object of interest is the policy function L⋆(z)≡arg⁡max⁡L∈P(L)f(L,z)\mathcal{L}^\star(z)\equiv\arg\max_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathcal{P}(L)}f(\mathcal{L},z)L⋆(z)≡argmaxL∈P(L)​f(L,z). The additional condition is single crossing differences in type (SCD-T): for all ℓ∈L\ell\in Lℓ∈L, all L∈P(L)\mathcal{L}\in\mathcal{P}(L)L∈P(L) and all types z<z′z<z'z<z′:

Dℓf(L,z)≥0  ⇒  Dℓf(L,z′)≥0(6.3.4.11)D_\ell f(\mathcal{L},z)\geq 0\;\Rightarrow\;D_\ell f(\mathcal{L},z')\geq 0 \tag{6.3.4.11}Dℓ​f(L,z)≥0⇒Dℓ​f(L,z′)≥0(6.3.4.11)

If an item is worth adding to a given set for some type, it is worth adding for all higher types. For each item and decision set there is then a single cutoff type, and the generalized version of Φ\PhiΦ only compares a type with this cutoff:

Φg(L,z)≡{ℓ∈L∣z≥zℓg(L)},zℓg(L)≡inf⁡{z∈R∣Dℓf(L,z)=0}(6.3.4.12)\Phi^g(\mathcal{L},z)\equiv\left\{\ell\in L\mid z\geq z^g_\ell(\mathcal{L})\right\},\qquad z^g_\ell(\mathcal{L})\equiv\inf\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}\mid D_\ell f(\mathcal{L},z)=0\right\} \tag{6.3.4.12}Φg(L,z)≡{ℓ∈L∣z≥zℓg​(L)},zℓg​(L)≡inf{z∈R∣Dℓ​f(L,z)=0}(6.3.4.12)

with zℓg(L)≡∞z^g_\ell(\mathcal{L})\equiv\inftyzℓg​(L)≡∞ if the marginal value is negative for all types and zℓg(L)≡−∞z^g_\ell(\mathcal{L})\equiv-\inftyzℓg​(L)≡−∞ if it is positive for all types. Bounding sets become bounding functions L‾(⋅)\underline{\mathcal{L}}(\cdot)L​(⋅) and L‾(⋅)\overline{\mathcal{L}}(\cdot)L(⋅) with L‾(z)⊆L⋆(z)⊆L‾(z)\underline{\mathcal{L}}(z)\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star(z)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}(z)L​(z)⊆L⋆(z)⊆L(z) for all zzz, and the generalized squeezing step is:

Sg([L(⋅),L′(⋅)])≡[inf⁡{Φg(L(⋅),⋅),Φg(L′(⋅),⋅)},  sup⁡{Φg(L(⋅),⋅),Φg(L′(⋅),⋅)}](6.3.4.13)S^g\left(\left[\mathcal{L}(\cdot),\mathcal{L}'(\cdot)\right]\right)\equiv\left[\inf\left\{\Phi^g\left(\mathcal{L}(\cdot),\cdot\right),\Phi^g\left(\mathcal{L}'(\cdot),\cdot\right)\right\},\;\sup\left\{\Phi^g\left(\mathcal{L}(\cdot),\cdot\right),\Phi^g\left(\mathcal{L}'(\cdot),\cdot\right)\right\}\right] \tag{6.3.4.13}Sg([L(⋅),L′(⋅)])≡[inf{Φg(L(⋅),⋅),Φg(L′(⋅),⋅)},sup{Φg(L(⋅),⋅),Φg(L′(⋅),⋅)}](6.3.4.13)

Any pair of bounding functions induces a partition T={Z1,…,ZT}\mathcal{T}=\{\mathcal{Z}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_T\}T={Z1​,…,ZT​} of the type space into intervals on which both bounding functions are constant, with values [L‾t,L‾t][\underline{\mathcal{L}}_t,\overline{\mathcal{L}}_t][L​t​,Lt​] on Zt\mathcal{Z}_tZt​.

Theorem 2. If fff exhibits SCD-C and SCD-T, iteratively applying the generalized squeezing step to the domain bounding functions [∅,L][\emptyset,L][∅,L] yields a sequence of bounding functions such that, for all z∈Rz\in\mathbb{R}z∈R:

∅⊆⋯⊆L‾(k)(z)⊆L‾(k+1)(z)⊆L⋆(z)⊆L‾(k+1)(z)⊆L‾(k)(z)⊆⋯⊆L(6.3.4.14)\emptyset\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}(z)\subseteq\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k+1)}(z)\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star(z)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k+1)}(z)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}(z)\subseteq\cdots\subseteq L \tag{6.3.4.14}∅⊆⋯⊆L​(k)(z)⊆L​(k+1)(z)⊆L⋆(z)⊆L(k+1)(z)⊆L(k)(z)⊆⋯⊆L(6.3.4.14)

and the iteration converges in K≤∣L∣K\leq|L|K≤∣L∣ applications.

For each type the step coincides with the squeezing step for the objective f(⋅,z)f(\cdot,z)f(⋅,z), so Theorem 1 gives the nesting, but SCD-T lets entire ranges of types be updated at once. With SCD-C from above, the first application computes for each ℓ\ellℓ the two cutoffs zℓg(∅)≤zℓg(L)z^g_\ell(\emptyset)\leq z^g_\ell(L)zℓg​(∅)≤zℓg​(L). Types below zℓg(∅)z^g_\ell(\emptyset)zℓg​(∅) do not want ℓ\ellℓ even when it stands alone, so ℓ\ellℓ is removed from their upper bounding set. Types above zℓg(L)z^g_\ell(L)zℓg​(L) want ℓ\ellℓ even when all other items are present, so ℓ\ellℓ is added to their lower bounding set. The cutoffs refine the partition, and later applications treat each interval separately. The reduced bounding functions pin down the policy function on every interval where they coincide.

Two refinements handle the remaining intervals. The generalized branching procedure branches on an item ℓ∈L‾t∖L‾t\ell\in\overline{\mathcal{L}}_t\setminus\underline{\mathcal{L}}_tℓ∈Lt​∖L​t​ as before, applies generalized squeezing on each branch, and chooses for each type the best of the conditionally optimal sets. Iterative cutoff search instead requires strong SCD-T: for any pair of decision sets (L,L′)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}')(L,L′) and types z<z′z<z'z<z′:

f(L,z)−f(L′,z)≥0  ⇒  f(L,z′)−f(L′,z′)>0(6.3.4.15)f(\mathcal{L},z)-f(\mathcal{L}',z)\geq 0\;\Rightarrow\;f(\mathcal{L},z')-f(\mathcal{L}',z')>0 \tag{6.3.4.15}f(L,z)−f(L′,z)≥0⇒f(L,z′)−f(L′,z′)>0(6.3.4.15)

so at most one type is indifferent between any two sets, and the policy function never returns to an earlier value as the type rises. On an interval with end points z<z′z<z'z<z′, if L⋆(z)=L⋆(z′)\mathcal{L}^\star(z)=\mathcal{L}^\star(z')L⋆(z)=L⋆(z′) the same set is optimal throughout. Otherwise the procedure finds the unique type z‾\overline{z}z that is indifferent between the two end-point sets and solves the CDCP at z‾\overline{z}z by squeezing and branching on the reduced domain. If L⋆(z‾)\mathcal{L}^\star(\overline{z})L⋆(z) equals one of the end-point sets, z‾\overline{z}z is the cutoff at which the policy function switches between them. If not, a third set lies in between, and the search repeats on [z,z‾][z,\overline{z}][z,z] and afterwards on the remainder of the interval. Generalized squeezing combined with a refinement is the policy function method. It locates the exact cutoffs at which the policy function changes value, wastes no computation on non-cutoff types, and needs no interpolation.

Multinational Production: Environment

The world consists of a set of countries LLL. A firm is headquartered in country iii, produces in a set of countries L⊆L\mathcal{L}\subseteq LL⊆L with typical element ℓ\ellℓ, and sells in every destination nnn. Each firm makes one differentiated variety with productivity zzz. In each country ℓ\ellℓ, HℓH_\ellHℓ​ households supply one unit of labor inelastically at wage wℓw_\ellwℓ​; labor markets are competitive and goods markets are monopolistically competitive. Complementarity versus Cannibalization

In a symmetric economy with ξiℓn=ξ\xi_{i\ell n}=\xiξiℓn​=ξ, the marginal value of a location depends only on the number of active locations:

Dℓπi(L,z)=Gzσ−1(∣L∪{ℓ}∣σ−1ε−1−∣L∖{ℓ}∣σ−1ε−1)−wℓfiℓ(6.3.4.21)D_\ell\pi_i(\mathcal{L},z)=\mathcal{G}z^{\sigma-1}\left(\left|\mathcal{L}\cup\{\ell\}\right|^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\varepsilon-1}}-\left|\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}\right|^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\varepsilon-1}}\right)-w_\ell f_{i\ell} \tag{6.3.4.21}Dℓ​πi​(L,z)=Gzσ−1(∣L∪{ℓ}∣ε−1σ−1​−∣L∖{ℓ}∣ε−1σ−1​)−wℓ​fiℓ​(6.3.4.21)

where G\mathcal{G}G is a composite general equilibrium constant. The ratio (σ−1)/(ε−1)(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)(σ−1)/(ε−1) is a sufficient statistic for the net effect of two opposing forces. On the demand side, σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 governs the ability to scale: the same proportional cost reduction yields a larger increase in sales for a firm that is already low-price, so each plant raises the value of the next (scale economies). On the cost side, ε>1\varepsilon>1ε>1 makes plants substitutes, since they compete with one another to supply each destination (cannibalization). If (σ−1)/(ε−1)>1(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)>1(σ−1)/(ε−1)>1, the marginal value of a location increases in the number of other locations, the profit function is supermodular and SCD-C from below holds. If (σ−1)/(ε−1)<1(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)<1(σ−1)/(ε−1)<1, it decreases, the profit function is submodular and SCD-C from above holds. If the ratio equals one, locations are independent. The CDCP requires both interdependence and fixed costs: with fiℓ=0f_{i\ell}=0fiℓ​=0 every marginal value is non-negative and all firms produce everywhere. A general equilibrium is a set of policy functions {Li⋆(⋅)}i\{\mathcal{L}^\star_i(\cdot)\}_i{Li⋆​(⋅)}i​ and aggregates {wi,z~i,Mi,Pi,Xi}i\{w_i,\tilde{z}_i,M_i,P_i,X_i\}_i{wi​,z~i​,Mi​,Pi​,Xi​}i​ such that the policy functions solve the firm problem given the aggregates and the aggregates satisfy the five conditions above given the policy functions. Because location sets differ across firms, the model has no closed-form aggregate gravity equation, and the policy functions must be recomputed at every guess of the aggregates.

Calibration

The data are averages for 2003 to 2012 of manufacturing trade flows, foreign affiliate sales and foreign affiliate counts for all pairs among 32 OECD and European countries (Alviarez 2019), supplemented by total firm counts (UNIDO), one-year firm survival rates (OECD), gravity variables (CEPII), tariffs, and GDP per capita and employment (Penn World Table). Two parameters are set externally. The demand elasticity is σ=4\sigma=4σ=4, following Arkolakis et al. (2018). The model is calibrated separately for 37 values of (σ−1)/(ε−1)(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)(σ−1)/(ε−1), evenly spaced between 0.25 and 3.9, which define the values of ε\varepsilonε. The substitutes benchmark is (σ−1)/(ε−1)=2/3(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)=2/3(σ−1)/(ε−1)=2/3, corresponding to ε=5.5\varepsilon=5.5ε=5.5 as in Arkolakis et al. (2018), and the complements benchmark is (σ−1)/(ε−1)=3/2(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)=3/2(σ−1)/(ε−1)=3/2, chosen for symmetry.

The remaining parameters are calibrated jointly. Productivity is Pareto with shape ζ\zetaζ and country-specific minimum z‾i\underline{z}_iz​i​; firm sales then have a Pareto tail of ζ/(σ−1)\zeta/(\sigma-1)ζ/(σ−1), and ζ=1.65×(σ−1)\zeta=1.65\times(\sigma-1)ζ=1.65×(σ−1) matches the tail estimate of Arkolakis (2010). The minimum z‾i\underline{z}_iz​i​ matches the share of global foreign production by firms headquartered in iii, and AℓA_\ellAℓ​ matches GDP per capita. Fixed costs are decomposed as fiℓ≡fiνiℓf_{i\ell}\equiv f_i\nu_{i\ell}fiℓ​≡fi​νiℓ​: the origin component fif_ifi​ matches the one-year survival rate, fief^e_ifie​ matches the mass of entrants (total firm count divided by the survival rate), and HℓH_\ellHℓ​ matches employment. The three bilateral matrices {τℓn}\{\tau_{\ell n}\}{τℓn​}, {γiℓ}\{\gamma_{i\ell}\}{γiℓ​} and {νiℓ}\{\nu_{i\ell}\}{νiℓ​} are constant-elasticity functions of distance and of indicators for a shared colonial past, a shared language and a common border, which gives twelve elasticities; tariffs enter trade costs with an elasticity of one, and γiℓ=∞\gamma_{i\ell}=\inftyγiℓ​=∞ for pairs with no MP in the data. The elasticities are identified by indirect inference: gravity regressions for trade flows, MP flows and affiliate counts are estimated by PPML on model-generated data, and the elasticities are chosen so that the coefficients match those in the actual data. The routine iterates on prices, fundamentals and bilateral costs, solving all policy functions at every guess, so that the observed wages, entrant masses and employment are an equilibrium; fief^e_ifie​ is recovered at the end from the free entry condition.

Computational Performance

Three experiments use the calibrated model, with up to 256 synthetic countries drawn from the distributions of the calibrated parameters and ordered by market size. The policy function method (generalized squeezing plus iterative cutoff search) is compared with two methods that discretize productivity on a grid of 2142^{14}214 points: a naive method that evaluates every location combination at every grid point, and a squeezing method that applies the squeezing procedure at each grid point and then brute force on the reduced domain. Reported times are averages across origin countries on a laptop processor. The discretization error of the grid-based squeezing method is measured against the exact policy function using trilateral flows XiℓnX_{i\ell n}Xiℓn​, the sales to nnn of plants in ℓ\ellℓ owned by firms from iii, and their grid-based counterparts X~iℓn\tilde{X}_{i\ell n}X~iℓn​, with NNN the number of countries:

error=N−3∑i,ℓ,n∈L∣X~iℓnXiℓn−1∣×100%(6.3.4.28)\text{error}=N^{-3}\sum_{i,\ell,n\in L}\left|\frac{\tilde{X}_{i\ell n}}{X_{i\ell n}}-1\right|\times 100\% \tag{6.3.4.28}error=N−3i,ℓ,n∈L∑​​Xiℓn​X~iℓn​​−1​×100%(6.3.4.28)

  • Speed: with 16 countries the naive method needs 5,215 seconds (complements) and 8,444 seconds (substitutes), the squeezing method 2.7 and 2.1 seconds, and the policy function method 0.087 and 0.018 seconds. With 32 countries the squeezing and policy methods take 17.0 versus 0.186 seconds (complements) and 10.7 versus 0.118 seconds (substitutes). With 128 countries they take 895 versus 14.7 and 874 versus 14.2 seconds, and with 256 countries 7,375 versus 374 and 4,797 versus 565 seconds. The naive method is infeasible beyond 16 countries. Relative to the incumbent in each case (grid-based squeezing for complements, brute force for substitutes), the gain is one to two orders of magnitude for complements and four to five for substitutes; about half of the latter comes from extending squeezing to substitutes and half from avoiding the grid.

  • Precision: with 512 grid points and 8 countries the average error exceeds 40 percent in both cases, and with more than 16,000 grid points it remains near or above 20 percent. Doubling the grid lowers the error by 5 to 10 percentage points and doubles the time. The error falls with the number of countries under complementarity, where the nested policy function means a grid misses only marginal additions, but not under substitutability, where firms between grid points may operate entirely different sets.

  • Applicability: across all 37 calibrations with 32 countries, the policy function takes under 0.1 seconds per origin on average. Computation is fastest when locations are close to independent. Squeezing time is nearly flat, in line with the bound of ∣L∣|L|∣L∣ applications in Theorem 2, and the time spent on refinement rises with the strength of complementarity or substitutability. After generalized squeezing, the average number of locations separating the upper and lower bounding sets is below 0.002.

Welfare Gains from Multinational Production

Each calibrated equilibrium is compared with an MP-autarky counterfactual with γiℓ=∞\gamma_{i\ell}=\inftyγiℓ​=∞ for all i≠ℓi\neq\elli=ℓ, in which firms produce only at home and the policy function reduces to the cutoffs z~i\tilde{z}_iz~i​. Let x^≡x/x′\hat{x}\equiv x/x'x^≡x/x′ denote the ratio of a variable in the calibrated equilibrium to its MP-autarky value. Following Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012), and assuming that all active firms produce in their headquarter country (true in all calibrations), the welfare change decomposes into three terms:

where ϕiii\phi_{iii}ϕiii​ is the share of country iii's expenditure on goods produced at home by firms headquartered in iii (an inverse measure of openness to trade and MP), and Ti={Zi,t}t\mathcal{T}_i=\{\mathcal{Z}_{i,t}\}_tTi​={Zi,t​}t​ is the partition of productivity into intervals on which Li⋆(⋅)\mathcal{L}^\star_i(\cdot)Li⋆​(⋅) is constant, with value Li,t\mathcal{L}_{i,t}Li,t​ and left end point zi,tz_{i,t}zi,t​. The shares are:

siℓi,t≡ξiℓi1−ε∑ℓ′∈Li,tξiℓ′i1−ε,λiii,t≡siii,tΘii(Li,t)σ−1ε−1[(zi,t)σ−1−ζ−(zi,t+1)σ−1−ζ]∑t′=1Tsiii,t′Θii(Li,t′)σ−1ε−1[(zi,t′)σ−1−ζ−(zi,t′+1)σ−1−ζ](6.3.4.30)s_{i\ell i,t}\equiv\frac{\xi_{i\ell i}^{1-\varepsilon}}{\sum_{\ell'\in\mathcal{L}_{i,t}}\xi_{i\ell'i}^{1-\varepsilon}},\qquad\lambda_{iii,t}\equiv\frac{s_{iii,t}\Theta_{ii}(\mathcal{L}_{i,t})^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\varepsilon-1}}\left[(z_{i,t})^{\sigma-1-\zeta}-(z_{i,t+1})^{\sigma-1-\zeta}\right]}{\sum_{t'=1}^{T}s_{iii,t'}\Theta_{ii}(\mathcal{L}_{i,t'})^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\varepsilon-1}}\left[(z_{i,t'})^{\sigma-1-\zeta}-(z_{i,t'+1})^{\sigma-1-\zeta}\right]} \tag{6.3.4.30}siℓi,t​≡∑ℓ′∈Li,t​​ξiℓ′i1−ε​ξiℓi1−ε​​,λiii,t​≡∑t′=1T​siii,t′​Θii​(Li,t′​)ε−1σ−1​[(zi,t′​)σ−1−ζ−(zi,t′+1​)σ−1−ζ]siii,t​Θii​(Li,t​)ε−1σ−1​[(zi,t​)σ−1−ζ−(zi,t+1​)σ−1−ζ]​(6.3.4.30)

so siℓi,ts_{i\ell i,t}siℓi,t​ is the share of the domestic sales of firms in interval ttt that is produced in ℓ\ellℓ, and λiii,t\lambda_{iii,t}λiii,t​ is the share of interval ttt in total domestic sales produced domestically.

  • Dispersion: at any degree of complementarity, gains from MP differ across countries because the fall in MP costs relative to autarky differs (the Netherlands gains much for this reason) and because countries differ in productivity as headquarters and as production sites. The cross-country distribution fans out as locations become more complementary. Gains in the United States triple between strong substitutability and strong complementarity, while Lithuania and Romania lose under strong complementarity.

  • Mechanism: complementarity strengthens multinational scale economies, so the most productive firms use their affiliates to cut marginal costs further and expand relative to other firms, and gains concentrate where they are headquartered. Countries that are weak as headquarters but attractive as production sites lose, because foreign affiliates crowd out domestic firms. Cannibalization under substitutability limits this concentration.

  • Mean versus median: the GDP-weighted average welfare gain is largest under the strongest complementarity, at 7.64 percent, whereas the median gain is largest under the strongest substitutability, at 6.70 percent.

  • Decomposition: the openness term is positive for all countries, and largest for heavy importers and for low-productivity economies that receive productive foreign affiliates. The variety term is negative for countries that mostly host foreign affiliates, where higher wages and survival cutoffs crowd out domestic entrants, and positive for headquarter countries such as the Netherlands and Finland; both effects are muted with substitutability. The average productivity term is positive and reflects reallocation of domestic market share toward multinationals. It is zero if no domestic firm engages in MP, and it is larger and more dispersed with complementarity.

  • Fixed costs: when the model is recalibrated without fixed costs, all firms produce everywhere, the concentration effect is weaker, and average gains from MP are larger in both benchmark cases, in line with Tintelnot (2017).

The operator DℓD_\ellDℓ​ is the discrete counterpart of a partial derivative. It answers one question: holding all other items in the decision set L\mathcal{L}L fixed, how much does the objective change when item ℓ\ellℓ is switched on instead of off? The first term evaluates fff with ℓ\ellℓ forced in, the second with ℓ\ellℓ forced out, so the value does not depend on whether ℓ\ellℓ itself belongs to L\mathcal{L}L:

Dℓf(L)=Dℓf(L∪{ℓ})=Dℓf(L∖{ℓ})D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})=D_\ell f\left(\mathcal{L}\cup\{\ell\}\right)=D_\ell f\left(\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}\right)Dℓ​f(L)=Dℓ​f(L∪{ℓ})=Dℓ​f(L∖{ℓ})

The units are those of fff (profits in the application). A positive value means that ℓ\ellℓ is worth having given the other items in L\mathcal{L}L, a negative value that it is not.

A three-item example that is reused in the other panels: let L={a,b,c}L=\{a,b,c\}L={a,b,c} and let every item have a stand-alone value vℓv_\ellvℓ​ while every pair of chosen items costs δ\deltaδ (these symbols are not in the note):

f(L)=∑ℓ∈Lvℓ−δ 12∣L∣(∣L∣−1),Dℓf(L)=vℓ−δ∣L∖{ℓ}∣f(\mathcal{L})=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}v_\ell-\delta\,\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathcal{L}|\left(|\mathcal{L}|-1\right),\qquad D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})=v_\ell-\delta\left|\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}\right|f(L)=ℓ∈L∑​vℓ​−δ21​∣L∣(∣L∣−1),Dℓ​f(L)=vℓ​−δ∣L∖{ℓ}∣

With (va,vb,vc)=(5,3,1)(v_a,v_b,v_c)=(5,3,1)(va​,vb​,vc​)=(5,3,1) and δ=2\delta=2δ=2 the items are substitutes: Dbf(∅)=3D_bf(\emptyset)=3Db​f(∅)=3, Dbf({a})=f({a,b})−f({a})=6−5=1D_bf(\{a\})=f(\{a,b\})-f(\{a\})=6-5=1Db​f({a})=f({a,b})−f({a})=6−5=1 and Dbf({a,c})=f({a,b,c})−f({a,c})=3−4=−1D_bf(\{a,c\})=f(\{a,b,c\})-f(\{a,c\})=3-4=-1Db​f({a,c})=f({a,b,c})−f({a,c})=3−4=−1. The same item is worth adding to a small set and not worth adding to a large one. With δ<0\delta<0δ<0 the items are complements and the marginal value rises with the number of other items.

This dependence of DℓfD_\ell fDℓ​f on the decision set is what makes the problem in equation (2) combinatorial. All later conditions are statements about the sign of DℓfD_\ell fDℓ​f: equation (3) restricts how the sign changes with the decision set, equation (11) how it changes with the agent type, and the mapping Φ\PhiΦ in equation (4) collects the items for which it is non-negative.

This defines the problem. The choice variable is a whole subset L\mathcal{L}L of the item set LLL, the feasible set P(L)\mathcal{P}(L)P(L) contains 2∣L∣2^{|L|}2∣L∣ subsets, and L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ is the subset with the highest payoff. With three items there are 8 candidates, with 20 items 220=1,048,5762^{20}=1{,}048{,}576220=1,048,576, and with the 32 countries of the application about 4.3×1094.3\times10^{9}4.3×109 for each firm type.

The problem is hard only because of interdependence. If the marginal value in equation (1) did not depend on the decision set, say Dℓf(L)=dℓD_\ell f(\mathcal{L})=d_\ellDℓ​f(L)=dℓ​ for every L\mathcal{L}L, then adding the items of L\mathcal{L}L one at a time would give

f(L)=f(∅)+∑ℓ∈Ldℓ⇒L⋆={ℓ∈L∣dℓ≥0}f(\mathcal{L})=f(\emptyset)+\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}d_\ell\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathcal{L}^\star=\left\{\ell\in L\mid d_\ell\geq0\right\}f(L)=f(∅)+ℓ∈L∑​dℓ​⇒L⋆={ℓ∈L∣dℓ​≥0}

and ∣L∣|L|∣L∣ separate comparisons would solve the problem. With interdependence the sign of DℓfD_\ell fDℓ​f depends on the other items, so each item can no longer be judged in isolation. In the three-item example of the panel for equation (1), with (va,vb,vc)=(5,3,1)(v_a,v_b,v_c)=(5,3,1)(va​,vb​,vc​)=(5,3,1) and δ=2\delta=2δ=2, the eight payoffs are f(∅)=0f(\emptyset)=0f(∅)=0, f({a})=5f(\{a\})=5f({a})=5, f({b})=3f(\{b\})=3f({b})=3, f({c})=1f(\{c\})=1f({c})=1, f({a,b})=6f(\{a,b\})=6f({a,b})=6, f({a,c})=4f(\{a,c\})=4f({a,c})=4, f({b,c})=2f(\{b,c\})=2f({b,c})=2 and f({a,b,c})=3f(\{a,b,c\})=3f({a,b,c})=3, so L⋆={a,b}\mathcal{L}^\star=\{a,b\}L⋆={a,b}. Every item has a positive stand-alone value, yet ccc is not chosen.

Two conventions matter later. First, when several subsets attain the maximum, L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ denotes the optimum that also contains the items over which the agent is indifferent; this is what makes Φ(L⋆)=L⋆\Phi(\mathcal{L}^\star)=\mathcal{L}^\starΦ(L⋆)=L⋆ hold in equation (4). Second, the method never enumerates P(L)\mathcal{P}(L)P(L). It brackets L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ between a lower and an upper bounding set and tightens the bracket, as in equations (5) to (8), and it branches only on the items that remain undetermined, as in equations (9) and (10).

Both lines restrict only the sign of the marginal value DℓfD_\ell fDℓ​f from equation (1) when the decision set grows from L\mathcal{L}L to a superset L′\mathcal{L}'L′, for every item ℓ\ellℓ.

From below: a non-negative marginal value in the smaller set stays non-negative in the larger set. Read along a chain of growing sets, the marginal value can pass from negative to non-negative but never back, so it crosses zero from below at most once. From above: a non-negative marginal value in the larger set is non-negative in the smaller set. The contrapositive is Dℓf(L)<0⇒Dℓf(L′)<0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})<0\Rightarrow D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')<0Dℓ​f(L)<0⇒Dℓ​f(L′)<0, so along a growing chain the marginal value can only pass from non-negative to negative.

The familiar cardinal conditions are sufficient. If fff is supermodular, then for L⊂L′\mathcal{L}\subset\mathcal{L}'L⊂L′

Dℓf(L′)≥Dℓf(L)≥0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')\geq D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\geq0Dℓ​f(L′)≥Dℓ​f(L)≥0

whenever the right-hand inequality holds, which is SCD-C from below; reversing the first inequality gives SCD-C from above under submodularity. In the example Dℓf(L)=vℓ−δ∣L∖{ℓ}∣D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})=v_\ell-\delta|\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}|Dℓ​f(L)=vℓ​−δ∣L∖{ℓ}∣ from the panel for equation (1), δ>0\delta>0δ>0 gives substitutes and SCD-C from above, δ<0\delta<0δ<0 gives complements and SCD-C from below.

The conditions are strictly weaker than the cardinal ones because magnitudes are free. Suppose the marginal value of item aaa is

Daf(∅)=−1,Daf({b})=3,Daf({b,c})=2D_af(\emptyset)=-1,\qquad D_af(\{b\})=3,\qquad D_af(\{b,c\})=2Da​f(∅)=−1,Da​f({b})=3,Da​f({b,c})=2

It rises and then falls, so fff is neither supermodular nor submodular, but the sign changes once, from negative to positive, which is all that SCD-C from below requires. SCD-C from above fails here, because Daf({b})≥0D_af(\{b\})\geq0Da​f({b})≥0 while Daf(∅)<0D_af(\emptyset)<0Da​f(∅)<0.

The role of the condition is to make the mapping Φ\PhiΦ of equation (4) monotone, order-preserving from below and order-reversing from above. That monotonicity is the only property used in equations (6) to (8). In the application the condition is verified in equation (22).

The mapping Φ\PhiΦ takes a decision set L\mathcal{L}L and returns the set of all items whose marginal value, computed with equation (1) given L\mathcal{L}L, is non-negative. It is a best-response map: taking the other items of L\mathcal{L}L as given, it asks separately for each item whether it should be in. Computing Φ(L)\Phi(\mathcal{L})Φ(L) costs ∣L∣|L|∣L∣ marginal values, that is, at most 2∣L∣2|L|2∣L∣ evaluations of fff, compared with 2∣L∣2^{|L|}2∣L∣ for brute force.

It is the discrete analogue of a first-order condition because the optimum is a fixed point. Take L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ to be an optimum that is maximal with respect to inclusion (the convention of the note). For an item inside and an item outside the optimum,

ℓ∈L⋆:Dℓf(L⋆)=f(L⋆)−f(L⋆∖{ℓ})≥0ℓ∉L⋆:Dℓf(L⋆)=f(L⋆∪{ℓ})−f(L⋆)<0\begin{aligned} \ell\in\mathcal{L}^\star:&\qquad D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}^\star)=f(\mathcal{L}^\star)-f\left(\mathcal{L}^\star\setminus\{\ell\}\right)\geq0\\ \ell\notin\mathcal{L}^\star:&\qquad D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}^\star)=f\left(\mathcal{L}^\star\cup\{\ell\}\right)-f(\mathcal{L}^\star)<0 \end{aligned}ℓ∈L⋆:ℓ∈/L⋆:​Dℓ​f(L⋆)=f(L⋆)−f(L⋆∖{ℓ})≥0Dℓ​f(L⋆)=f(L⋆∪{ℓ})−f(L⋆)<0​

The first line holds because no subset beats L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆. The second is strict because otherwise L⋆∪{ℓ}\mathcal{L}^\star\cup\{\ell\}L⋆∪{ℓ} would be a larger optimum. Hence Φ(L⋆)=L⋆\Phi(\mathcal{L}^\star)=\mathcal{L}^\starΦ(L⋆)=L⋆. As with a first-order condition, the converse fails: a fixed point of Φ\PhiΦ only rules out single-item deviations and need not be the global optimum.

In the substitutes example of the panel for equation (1), Dℓf(L)=vℓ−2∣L∖{ℓ}∣D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})=v_\ell-2|\mathcal{L}\setminus\{\ell\}|Dℓ​f(L)=vℓ​−2∣L∖{ℓ}∣ with (va,vb,vc)=(5,3,1)(v_a,v_b,v_c)=(5,3,1)(va​,vb​,vc​)=(5,3,1):

Φ(∅)={a,b,c},Φ({a})={a,b},Φ({a,b})={a,b},Φ({a,b,c})={a}\Phi(\emptyset)=\{a,b,c\},\qquad\Phi(\{a\})=\{a,b\},\qquad\Phi(\{a,b\})=\{a,b\},\qquad\Phi(\{a,b,c\})=\{a\}Φ(∅)={a,b,c},Φ({a})={a,b},Φ({a,b})={a,b},Φ({a,b,c})={a}

The set {a,b}\{a,b\}{a,b} is the fixed point and the optimum. The example also shows that Φ\PhiΦ is order-reversing here: larger arguments give smaller images. Under SCD-C from above this is general, and under SCD-C from below Φ\PhiΦ is order-preserving; see equation (3). The squeezing step in equations (5) and (6) is built entirely from Φ\PhiΦ, and equation (12) gives its version for a continuum of types.

The squeezing step takes a pair of decision sets, in practice the current lower and upper bounding sets, applies the mapping Φ\PhiΦ of equation (4) to each of them, and returns the two images ordered as a new pair. The order is set inclusion, so for two sets that are nested the infimum is the smaller and the supremum is the larger; in general, on the lattice of subsets,

inf⁡{A,B}=A∩B,sup⁡{A,B}=A∪B\inf\left\{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\right\}=\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{B},\qquad\sup\left\{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\right\}=\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{B}inf{A,B}=A∩B,sup{A,B}=A∪B

The first element of the output is the new lower bounding set (items now known to be chosen) and the second is the new upper bounding set (items outside it are now known not to be chosen).

The definition is written with inf⁡\infinf and sup⁡\supsup so that it does not need to know which type of SCD-C holds. Under SCD-C the two images Φ(L)\Phi(\mathcal{L})Φ(L) and Φ(L′)\Phi(\mathcal{L}')Φ(L′) are always nested, and equation (6) shows which one is the smaller in each case. One step requires 2∣L∣2|L|2∣L∣ marginal values.

In the substitutes example of the panel for equation (1) (three items, Φ(∅)={a,b,c}\Phi(\emptyset)=\{a,b,c\}Φ(∅)={a,b,c} and Φ({a,b,c})={a}\Phi(\{a,b,c\})=\{a\}Φ({a,b,c})={a}), the first step applied to the whole domain gives

so item aaa is fixed in the optimum after a single step and the candidates fall from 8 to 4. Why the output is again a valid bracket of L⋆\mathcal{L}^\starL⋆ is shown in the panel for equation (7). Iterating SSS until nothing changes is the squeezing procedure, and equation (13) is the same step applied to all agent types at once.

The economic reading is that the bounds cross over in the substitutes case. The new lower bound comes from the old upper bound, because an item that is still worth having when every admissible rival is present is certainly chosen; the new upper bound comes from the old lower bound, because an item that is not worth having even next to the fewest admissible rivals is certainly not chosen. In the complements case each bound updates itself.

The converse of Steps 1 and 2 also holds, so Φ\PhiΦ is monotone if and only if fff satisfies SCD-C. For instance, if Φ\PhiΦ is order-preserving and Dℓf(L)≥0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L})\geq0Dℓ​f(L)≥0, then ℓ∈Φ(L)⊆Φ(L′)\ell\in\Phi(\mathcal{L})\subseteq\Phi(\mathcal{L}')ℓ∈Φ(L)⊆Φ(L′), which says Dℓf(L′)≥0D_\ell f(\mathcal{L}')\geq0Dℓ​f(L′)≥0.

This is Theorem 1. The proof needs three facts: the fixed-point property Φ(L⋆)=L⋆\Phi(\mathcal{L}^\star)=\mathcal{L}^\starΦ(L⋆)=L⋆ from the panel for equation (4), the monotonicity of Φ\PhiΦ, and the simplified squeezing step in equation (6). The case of SCD-C from above is written out; the other case is noted at the end.

Step 1, the squeezing step never discards the optimum. Suppose L‾(k)⊆L⋆⊆L‾(k)\underline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}\subseteq\mathcal{L}^\star\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{L}}^{(k)}L​(k)⊆L⋆⊆L(k), which is true for k=0k=0k=0. SCD-T is the counterpart of equation (3) in the type dimension. It fixes an item ℓ\ellℓ and a decision set L\mathcal{L}L and compares two agents with types z<z′z<z'z<z′: if the lower type weakly gains from having ℓ\ellℓ next to the other items of L\mathcal{L}L, so does the higher type. As a function of zzz, the marginal value Dℓf(L,z)D_\ell f(\mathcal{L},z)Dℓ​f(L,z) therefore crosses zero at most once, and from below. It may be non-monotone in zzz and may even stay at zero on an interval; only the sign pattern is restricted.

What the condition buys is a cutoff rule. Together with continuity of fff in zzz, the set of types that want ℓ\ellℓ given L\mathcal{L}L is an upper interval,

{z∈R∣Dℓf(L,z)≥0}=[zℓg(L),∞)\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}\mid D_\ell f(\mathcal{L},z)\geq0\right\}=\left[z^g_\ell(\mathcal{L}),\infty\right){z∈R∣Dℓ​f(L,z)≥0}=[zℓg​(L),∞)

so one number per pair (ℓ,L)(\ell,\mathcal{L})(ℓ,L) summarizes the decision of all types. The condition does not say that higher types choose larger sets: the cutoff of ℓ\ellℓ depends on L\mathcal{L}L, and under substitutes a higher type may drop an item when it adds others.

Strong SCD-T strengthens equation (11) in two ways. It compares any two decision sets, not only a set with and without one item, and the conclusion is a strict inequality. If L\mathcal{L}L is weakly preferred to L′\mathcal{L}'L′ by some type, it is strictly preferred by every higher type. As a function of zzz, the payoff difference f(L,z)−f(L′,z)f(\mathcal{L},z)-f(\mathcal{L}',z)f(L,z)−f(L′,z) then has at most one zero, so at most one type is indifferent between the two sets.

A remark on how to read the statement. The implication is directional and has to be understood for the appropriate labelling of each pair: the set called L\mathcal{L}L is the one that higher types favour. If the implication held for both labellings of the same pair, the ranking of two sets could never switch as zzz rises and the policy function would be constant. The content of the condition, in the paper's words, is that the payoff difference of any pair crosses zero for at most one type.

Why it implies that the policy function never returns to an earlier value: suppose A\mathcal{A}A is optimal at z1z_1z1​ and at z3z_3z3​ and a different set B\mathcal{B}B is optimal at z2z_2z2​, with z1<z2<z3z_1<z_2<z_3z1​<z2​<z3​ (symbols not used in the note). Then

f(A,z1)−f(B,z1)≥0,f(A,z2)−f(B,z2)≤0,f(A,z3)−f(B,z3)≥0f(\mathcal{A},z_1)-f(\mathcal{B},z_1)\geq0,\qquad f(\mathcal{A},z_2)-f(\mathcal{B},z_2)\leq0,\qquad f(\mathcal{A},z_3)-f(\mathcal{B},z_3)\geq0f(A,z1​)−f(B,z1​)≥0,f(A,z2​)−f(B,z2​)≤0,f(A,z3​)−f(B,z3​)≥0

If A\mathcal{A}A is the set favoured by higher types, the first inequality forces a strict preference for A\mathcal{A}A at z2z_2z2​, contradicting the second; if it is B\mathcal{B}B, the second forces a strict preference for B\mathcal{B}B at z3z_3z3​, contradicting the third. Each decision set is therefore optimal on a single interval of types. This is what iterative cutoff search exploits: on an interval whose end points have different optimal sets it computes the unique type z‾\overline{z}z indifferent between the two end-point sets and solves a single CDCP there.

This is the technology assumption of the application. A firm headquartered in iii with productivity zzz that operates the location set L\mathcal{L}L serves destination nnn at a constant marginal cost cinc_{in}cin​. Everything is paid in the labor of the producing country, which matters for equation (26). Productivity zzz lowers cost proportionally at all plants.

A microfoundation: the final good needs a continuum of inputs, each plant draws an input-specific efficiency from a Frechet distribution with shape ε−1\varepsilon-1ε−1, and every input for destination nnn is sourced from the cheapest plant. The expected cost is then the CES aggregator above, up to a constant, and ξiℓn1−ε/Θin(L)\xi_{i\ell n}^{1-\varepsilon}/\Theta_{in}(\mathcal{L})ξiℓn1−ε​/Θin​(L) is the fraction of inputs supplied by plant ℓ\ellℓ. The form rules out plant-level capacity constraints and increasing marginal cost. It is what generates cannibalization: plants compete for the same destinations, and the interaction with demand in equations (20) to (22) depends only on the ratio (σ−1)/(ε−1)(\sigma-1)/(\varepsilon-1)(σ−1)/(ε−1).

The problem is a two-stage one. Prices are chosen optimally for any given L\mathcal{L}L, so the outer problem is a pure choice of a subset of LLL: a CDCP in the sense of equation (2) with items LLL, objective f=πif=\pi_if=πi​ and type zzz. The trade-off is that a larger set lowers cinc_{in}cin​ in every destination and raises revenue, while every plant adds its own fixed cost. The fixed costs enter additively and create no interdependence; the revenue term is a nonlinear function of the whole set, made explicit in equation (20). Note also that the empty set is feasible and gives zero revenue and zero cost, which is the exit option behind the cutoff in equation (23).

The condition is called balance of payments because it rules out a deficit or surplus. Country nnn may import more goods than it exports, but then the difference is paid for by the profits that its multinationals repatriate, and with zero net profits in the aggregate the current account is balanced. This is the accuracy measure of the computational experiments, not a model equation. The object XiℓnX_{i\ell n}Xiℓn​ is the value of sales to destination nnn produced in plants located in ℓ\ellℓ that belong to firms headquartered in iii; it is the integral of the location share times firm sales that appears in equation (26). It is computed twice: exactly, with the policy function Li⋆(⋅)\mathcal{L}^\star_i(\cdot)Li⋆​(⋅) and its exact cutoffs, and approximately, as X~iℓn\tilde{X}_{i\ell n}X~iℓn​, by solving the CDCP only at the points of a productivity grid and integrating with the grid.

For each triple the term inside the sum is the absolute percentage deviation of the grid-based flow from the exact one. With NNN countries there are N3N^3N3 triples, so the factor N−3N^{-3}N−3 makes the statistic the simple average over all of them, in percent. Three features of the construction matter. Absolute values prevent positive and negative deviations from cancelling. The average is unweighted, so a small flow that is badly approximated counts as much as a large one, and the statistic is therefore not the error in a typical aggregate such as a country's total output. And the deviation is relative, so it presumes Xiℓn>0X_{i\ell n}>0Xiℓn​>0; triples with a prohibitive MP cost, for which both flows are zero, have to be left out or counted as zero.

Why a grid produces an error at all: the policy function is a step function of zzz, and a grid assigns to all types between two grid points the location set of a grid point. If the true cutoff at which a firm adds or drops location ℓ\ellℓ lies between grid points, a range of firms is assigned the wrong status for ℓ\ellℓ. For example, with N=2N=2N=2 there are 8 triples; if two of them are off by 30 percent, two by 10 percent and four are exact, the statistic is (2×30+2×10)/8=10(2\times30+2\times10)/8=10(2×30+2×10)/8=10 percent. Because productivity is Pareto and sales are proportional to zσ−1z^{\sigma-1}zσ−1, a thin range of high types can carry a large share of a flow, which is why the reported errors stay near or above 20 percent even with 2142^{14}214 grid points. Under substitutes a firm between grid points may use an entirely different set, so the error does not shrink as countries are added. The policy function method has no such error because it computes the cutoffs themselves.

Interpretation. A firm with home share sss has marginal cost ξiiis1/(ε−1)/z\xi_{iii}s^{1/(\varepsilon-1)}/zξiii​s1/(ε−1)/z in its home market, lower than a purely domestic firm, exactly as a lower domestic trade share signals lower prices in Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012). The openness term is that logic applied to ϕiii\phi_{iii}ϕiii​; the variety term records the change in the mass of entrants and in the surviving fraction; the average productivity term records selection through z~i\tilde{z}_iz~i​ and the cost reductions of multinationals. It is an accounting identity given the equilibrium values of the four statistics, not a causal split.
